title: One auxiliary, not two
summary: The essere/avere choice simply does not exist in Spanish.
body: Italian makes you choose an auxiliary for every compound tense, and then agree the participle when it is essere. Spanish has one auxiliary, **haber**, for every verb without exception — and the participle never agrees.
This is the single biggest simplification Spanish offers you. Movement verbs, reflexives, **ser** itself: all take haber.
watch: Your instinct will produce *soy ido* and *somos idos*. There is no context in which that is right.

title: Which past tense to reach for
summary: Italian's everyday past maps to the Spanish preterite, not the perfect.
body: In Italian the **passato prossimo** is the ordinary past and the passato remoto is literary or southern. So your instinct is: past → compound tense.

In Latin American Spanish that instinct is wrong. The ordinary past is the simple **pretérito**. The compound **pretérito perfecto** exists and looks exactly like the passato prossimo, which is the trap: it is used far less.
This affects nearly every past-tense sentence you will say, which makes it the highest-frequency error available to you.
watch: In Spain `he comido hoy` is normal and much closer to Italian. You chose Latin American, so the preterite is your default.

title: Possessives take no article
summary: il mio libro → mi libro. Spanish never puts an article there.
body: Italian requires the definite article before a possessive: *il mio libro*, *la tua casa*. Spanish never does.
Italian's own exception — dropping the article for singular unmodified family members, *mio fratello* — is a rule you can forget entirely, because Spanish treats every noun the same way.
Spanish also has a second, stressed possessive that goes **after** the noun: *un amigo mío*, *¿es tuyo?* That is the form that looks like Italian's.
pairs: same in Spanish, no exception needed
watch: *el mi libro* is the error, and it is one you will make.

title: There is no partitive
summary: del pane, dei libri → just pan, libros.
body: Italian uses *del*, *della*, *dei*, *delle* to mean 'some'. Spanish has no partitive at all. Where Italian puts a word, Spanish puts nothing.
This one is easy to fix because the correction is always deletion.
watch: *Quiero del pan* is wrong. So is *compré de los libros*.

title: ser and estar are not essere and stare
summary: The concept transfers; the boundary does not.
body: Italian has essere and stare, so the idea of two 'to be' verbs is familiar. The problem is that the line falls in a different place, and the cognate pull is towards the wrong one.
**estar** covers location, and temporary or changed states — including many that Italian expresses with essere.
**ser** covers identity, origin, material, time, and inherent qualities.
Location is the clearest rule: things and people are **estar**. The one exception is events, which use ser: *la fiesta es en mi casa*.
pairs: La festa è a casa mia.
La fiesta es en mi casa.
watch: *soy cansado* means something like 'I am a tiring person'. *soy en casa* is simply wrong.

title: avere does two jobs; Spanish uses two verbs
summary: Italian's avere is both 'to have' and the auxiliary. Spanish splits them: tener owns things, haber builds tenses.
body: This is the single most reliable trap for an Italian speaker, because **avere** is one verb doing two jobs and Spanish never lets them touch. *Ho una casa* and *ho parlato* use the same verb in Italian. In Spanish the first is **tener** and the second is **haber**, and swapping them is not a small mistake — *tengo hablado* is not a sentence.
The rule is clean: if you can point at the thing, it is **tener**. If it is holding up a participle, it is **haber**. Spanish speakers never say *he un coche* and never say *tengo comido*.

Where Italian says **avere** in a fixed expression about how you feel, Spanish almost always says **tener** — and this transfers perfectly, so it is free vocabulary. Hunger, thirst, cold, fear, sleepiness, and your age are all things you *have* in both languages, which English gets wrong and you already get right.

**haber** has one more job with no Italian parallel worth the name: the impersonal **hay**, meaning there is or there are. Italian chooses between *c'è* and *ci sono*; Spanish does not. **hay** never changes for number — *hay un libro*, *hay dos libros*. Never *han*.

Finally, the false friend. Italian **tenere** is not Spanish **tener**. *Tenere* is to hold or to keep — *tieni questo* is *sujeta esto*. If you reach for tenere expecting possession you will be reaching for the wrong idea, even though the word looks right.
pairs: tenere is to hold, not to have
watch: Your instinct will produce *tengo hablado* for *ho parlato*, and *he hambre* for *ho fame*. Both are wrong in the same way: you carried avere across whole instead of choosing which of its two jobs you meant.

title: dovere splits three ways
summary: Obligation, debt and guesswork are one verb in Italian and three constructions in Spanish.
body: Italian **dovere** carries three meanings at once: I have to, I owe, and it must be. Spanish separates them, and the everyday one is not the cognate.

For ordinary obligation Spanish reaches for **tener que**, not **deber**. *Devo andare* is **tengo que ir**. You will be understood if you say *debo ir*, but it sounds weightier — closer to a duty than to a plan. Save **deber** for moral obligation: *debes respetar a tus padres*.
For owing, **deber** is exactly right and the cognate holds: *ti devo dieci euro* is **te debo diez euros**.

For supposition — the *deve essere* sense, guessing at a cause — careful Spanish uses **deber de**: *debe de estar cansado*. The *de* is dropped constantly in speech, and nobody will misunderstand you, but the distinction is the one the grammar books defend.
The pattern to carry away: **tener que** is what you will need most, and it is the one your Italian will not suggest to you.
pairs: you must not — a different meaning
watch: *Devo andare* → *debo ir* is the mistake you will make most often. It is not wrong, it is just heavier than you mean. Spanish says **tengo que**.

title: The personal a
summary: Spanish marks a human direct object with a. Italian has nothing like it.
body: When the direct object of a verb is a specific person, Spanish puts **a** in front of it. Italian does not, and there is no equivalent to transfer from.
It applies to people and to pets, not to things. It also applies to *alguien*, *nadie*, and to *quién* in questions.
watch: Omitting it is the classic Italian-speaker error, and it is audible in every sentence about a person.

title: per splits into por and para
summary: One Italian preposition, two Spanish ones, and the choice is obligatory.
body: Italian *per* does several jobs. Spanish divides them between **por** and **para**, and you must pick.
**para** points forwards: destination, purpose, recipient, deadline.
**por** points backwards or through: cause, exchange, duration, means, movement through a place.
The shortest test that works most of the time: *para* answers 'what for?', *por* answers 'why?' or 'in exchange for what?'
watch: There is no safe default. Guessing *por* everywhere is wrong about half the time.

title: Where things are, and where you are going
summary: Italian's a/in/da do not line up with Spanish a/en/de.
body: Italian chooses between *a* and *in* partly by the kind of place — *a Roma* but *in Italia*. Spanish chooses by whether there is movement.
**en** for being somewhere, whatever the place. **a** for going there.
Italian *da* has no single Spanish equivalent. For a person's place it becomes *en casa de* or *a casa de*; for origin it becomes *de*.
watch: *Estoy a Roma* and *voy en Roma* are the two errors, and they are mirror images of each other.

title: ne and ci do not exist
summary: Two Italian pronouns with no Spanish counterpart at all.
body: Italian *ne* ('of it', 'of them') and locative *ci* ('there') have no Spanish equivalents. Spanish either repeats the noun or says nothing.
The risk is not getting them wrong — it is inventing something to carry them.
watch: **hay** is invariable. *Han dos libros* is a very common error.

title: Words that changed gender
summary: Most nouns keep their gender. These did not.
body: Gender transfers almost perfectly, which makes the exceptions worth memorising individually — there are not many, and you will otherwise get them wrong every time.
Nouns ending in -aje, -or and -ma (from Greek) are masculine in Spanish; nouns in -umbre, -dad, -tad and -ción are feminine.
watch: *el sangre* and *la origen* are the shape of this error.

title: How the words changed shape
summary: Most vocabulary transfers by rule. Learn the rule, not the words.
body: Italian and Spanish share the great majority of their vocabulary, and the differences are largely regular. Recognising the correspondences turns thousands of Italian words into Spanish ones.
Spanish has **no double consonants** except rr, ll, cc and nn. Italian's doubles simplify.
watch: Doubling a consonant is the most audible Italian accent in Spanish.

title: Adjectives that drop their ending
summary: Both languages shorten a few adjectives before a noun — but not the same ones, and not to the same degree.
body: Italian already does this, so the idea is familiar: you say **un buon caffè**, not *un buono caffè*, and **un gran problema** rather than *un grande problema*. Spanish does the same thing, more systematically, and the list of words it applies to is not identical.

The Spanish rule is tighter than the Italian one. **bueno**, **malo**, **primero**, **tercero**, **alguno** and **ninguno** drop their final **-o** before a masculine singular noun, and only there. **grande** shortens to **gran** before a singular noun of either gender. **ciento** becomes **cien** before any noun, and before **mil** and **millones**.

Two differences will catch you out. Spanish shortens only before the noun it modifies, never after it and never standing alone — *el libro es bueno*, never *es buen*. And **grande** changes meaning when it moves: **un gran hombre** is a great man, **un hombre grande** is a big one. Italian has the same split with **grande**, so trust that instinct.

Where Italian is looser, Spanish is stricter. Italian lets **bello**, **santo** and **quello** take a whole family of shapes depending on the sound that follows — *bel libro*, *bell'uomo*, *begli occhi*. Spanish has nothing of this: **bello** never shortens, and **santo** shortens to **san** only before a man's name, not before ordinary nouns.

One apocopation is not optional and not positional: **muy** and **mucho**. Spanish uses **muy** before an adjective or another adverb — *muy alto*, *muy bien* — and **mucho** before a noun or after a verb — *mucho tiempo*, *trabaja mucho*. You cannot swap them the way you can hesitate between *gran* and *grande*. Italian makes no such split: **molto** does all of it, which is why this one has to be learned rather than transferred.
pairs: after the noun: big, not great
watch: The trap is assuming the two lists match. Italian shortens **bello** and Spanish does not; Spanish shortens **grande** before feminine nouns and Italian will not. Your ear offers *un bel libro* and Spanish has no such form — it wants **un libro bonito**. And Italian's single **molto** will offer you *muy tiempo* or *mucho alto*; Spanish splits what Italian does not.

title: Words that lie to you
summary: The small set where the cognate is actively wrong.
body: These are dangerous precisely because you will say them with confidence. There are not many, and they are worth learning as a list.
watch: *Quiero burro en el pan* asks for donkey on your bread.

title: Where the words go
summary: Freer than English, and mostly like Italian — until it isn't.
body: Both languages let you move things around for emphasis, and both drop the subject pronoun by default. Most of your instincts carry over.

Two places they part company. Spanish **inverts the subject in questions** far more consistently than Italian, which often relies on intonation alone. And Spanish will not split a compound verb: nothing goes between **haber** and the participle.
Adjectives normally follow the noun in both. Moving one in front changes the sense the same way in both languages: *un hombre pobre* is penniless, *un pobre hombre* is pitiable.
pairs: nothing between haber and the participle
watch: *He siempre dicho* is the error, and it comes straight from Italian word order.

title: Asking and exclaiming
summary: Spanish opens a question with an upside-down mark, and closes it.
body: Every question is wrapped: **¿...?** And every exclamation: **¡...!** The opening mark goes where the question actually starts, which is not always the start of the sentence.
Question words carry a written accent — *qué*, *dónde*, *cuándo*, *quién*, *cómo*, *cuánto* — and lose it when they are not questioning.
pairs: the mark opens at the question
watch: Leaving off the opening ¿ is the most visible way to write Spanish like an Italian.

title: Two pronouns in a row
summary: le + lo becomes se lo. Italian has nothing that behaves like it.
body: Placement works as it does in Italian: before a conjugated verb, attached to an infinitive, a gerund or an affirmative command.

The difference is what happens when two third-person pronouns meet. Italian turns *gli* + *lo* into *glielo*. Spanish turns **le** + **lo** into **se lo** — the indirect pronoun is replaced outright by *se*.
Latin America keeps **lo** and **la** for the direct object of a person. Spain often uses *le* for a man; you can ignore that.
pairs: attached to the command, with an accent added
watch: *Le lo doy* is never right. It is always *se lo doy*.

title: The many uses of se
summary: Reflexive, impersonal, passive — and the replacement for le.
body: Spanish *se* does the work of Italian *si*, and the two line up closely: reflexive, impersonal, and passive.
The impersonal is everywhere in Spanish, on signs and in speech, where English would use 'you' or a passive.
pairs: agrees with the plural, as in Italian
watch: This one transfers almost perfectly. The only se that will surprise you is the one standing in for le.

title: gustar works like piacere
summary: The structure is the same. The doubling is not.
body: *Me gusta el café* is built exactly like *mi piace il caffè*: the thing liked is the subject, and you are the indirect object. That transfers without effort.
What Spanish adds is a habit of **doubling** the pronoun with *a mí*, *a ti*, *a Ana* — for emphasis, contrast, or simply because it sounds right. Italian does this far less.
The same pattern runs through a family of verbs: *encantar*, *interesar*, *parecer*, *faltar*, *doler*.
pairs: A me piace, a lui no.
A mí me gusta, a él no.
A Ana le gusta el cine.
watch: *Mi manca* is the trap: Spanish *me falta* means something is lacking, not that you miss it. To miss someone is **extrañar**.

title: Diminutives, and how much they matter
summary: -ito is everywhere in Mexico, and not always about size.
body: Italian has -ino, -etto, -ello. Spanish has **-ito** and **-illo**, and in Mexico -ito is used constantly — for affection, for politeness, for softening a request, and only sometimes for size.
*Ahorita* is the one to know. Literally 'right now', in practice anywhere from this second to never.
pairs: softened, and vaguer than it looks
watch: Using no diminutives at all reads as brusque in Mexico, in a way it would not in Italy.

title: Possessives drop the article
summary: Italian says il mio libro. Spanish says mi libro, and never the other way.
body: Italian puts an article in front of a possessive almost everywhere: *il mio libro*, *la tua casa*, *i nostri amici*. Spanish does not. The possessive stands alone — **mi libro**, **tu casa**, **nuestros amigos** — and adding *el* or *la* in front of it is simply wrong.

The short forms — mi, tu, su, nuestro — go before the noun and agree only in number, except nuestro/vuestro which agree in gender too. There is no masculine/feminine difference in mi, tu or su at all: *mi hermano* and *mi hermana* both.
There is also a long form that goes after the noun — **mío, tuyo, suyo** — used for emphasis, after ser, and in direct address. That one does agree in gender and number.

**Su** is the one that will trip you. It covers his, her, your (usted), their — everything Italian splits between *suo* and *loro*. Spanish leaves it ambiguous and clarifies with *de él*, *de ella*, *de usted* when the context does not.
pairs: mi does not change for gender
loro collapses into su as well
the long form survives in exclamations
watch: *El mi libro* and *la mi casa* are the errors to watch for, and they will feel natural for a long time. The other one is reaching for a plural to translate *loro* — Spanish has no separate word, and su does that work too.
